title: Argentinian Chimichurri Steak
subtitle: grilled beef with fresh herb sauce
excerpt: A thick steak cooked in a very hot cast-iron pan, served with chimichurri -- a bright, pungent sauce of parsley, oregano, garlic, and red wine vinegar. Simple cooking, bold flavours.
sourceNotes: Chimichurri is the defining sauce of Argentinian and Uruguayan BBQ culture. The name's origin is debated, but the sauce -- parsley, garlic, olive oil, and vinegar -- has been an asado staple for generations.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the chimichurri up to 2 days ahead. It deepens in flavour.

content.text: Get the pan as hot as possible before the steak goes in. Do not move the steak once it hits the pan. Let it form a crust before turning. Rest the steak for at least half the cooking time.

items.prepNote: use 4 rump or sirloin steaks, about 200g each

content.text: Make the chimichurri: mix the parsley, garlic, oregano, chilli flakes, red wine vinegar, and olive oil. Season with salt. Set aside.
Pat the steaks dry. Rub with oil and season generously with salt flakes.
Heat a cast-iron skillet over very high heat until smoking.
Cook the steaks for 2 to 3 minutes per side for medium-rare. Do not press them down or move them until they release naturally.
Rest the steaks on a board for at least 10 minutes before cutting.
Slice the rested steak against the grain. Spoon chimichurri generously over the top.

items.cause: Pan not hot enough or steak moved too early
items.fix: A hot pan creates a crust that releases naturally. If it feels stuck, it is not ready to turn yet. Wait 30 more seconds.

items.cause: Cut with the grain or not rested
items.fix: Always cut across the grain of the meat. Resting allows the fibres to relax and the juices to redistribute.
Balance with a little extra olive oil and a pinch of salt. The sauce should be punchy but not harsh.

content.text: Chimichurri is the soul of the Argentinian asado. Argentinians take their grilled meat very seriously, and chimichurri is always there alongside it. The sauce is also widely used in Uruguay and other parts of South America. The asado tradition gathers family and friends around an open fire, and it is one of the most important social rituals in Argentinian life.
